title: Increasing Governmental Efficacy Beliefs Drives Support for Congestion Pricing Policy
description: Congestion pricing charges drivers a fee to enter high-traffic areas, reducing congestion and travel times while generating revenue for public transit and lowering air pollution and greenhouse gas emissions. Despite its effectiveness, the policy remains contentious because it imposes immediate, salient personal costs in exchange for benefits that are less tangible, delayed, and distributed across both individuals (e.g., shorter, more reliable trips) and society (e.g., cleaner air, safer streets, and improved public transit). This asymmetry between how costs and benefits are experienced poses a challenge to public support, which is essential for both the adoption and long-term durability of the policy. Across two large-scale experiments conducted in New York State (N = 15,014) and Washington, D.C. (N = 4,030), we tested 24 psychologically informed interventions designed to increase support for congestion pricing. Increasing governmental outcome efficacy beliefs, by emphasizing that the policy enables government to deliver meaningful public benefits, emerged as the most effective strategy, increasing support for congestion pricing by 30%, while also improving perceptions of the policy's effectiveness and fairness. These effects were robust across intervention delivery modes that varied in participant engagement and did not differ by political affiliation. Together, these findings identify policy-specific outcome efficacy as a scalable and politically robust communication strategy for building public support for sustainable transportation policies.

title: How Social Context Shapes Perceived Identity Overlap:  Evidence from Christian Democrats
description: Why do some people perceive two social identities as fitting together while others see them as largely distinct? We propose that these perceptions are shaped, in part, by the social environments in which people live. We tested this model using Christian Democrats, whose religious and political identities often violate prevailing partisan stereotypes. Two observational studies (Ns = 505 and 484) showed that local political (Democratic voting margins) and religious (Christian prevalence) contexts predicted perceived support for Christian and Democratic identities. Specifically, living in more Democratic counties was associated with greater perceived support for Democrats and lower perceived support for Christians, whereas living in more Christian counties was generally associated with greater perceived support for Christians and lower perceived support for Democrats. In turn, greater perceived support for either identity was associated with perceiving Christian and Democratic identities as more overlapping. Consistent with this model, a preregistered experiment (N = 769) demonstrated that increasing perceived support for Christians increased perceived overlap between Christian and Democratic identities. Across studies, greater perceived overlap was selectively associated with warmer evaluations of Christian and Republican targets, suggesting that when people perceive their identities as not fitting together, they may reaffirm one identity (e.g., Democrat) by distancing themselves from the competing identity (e.g., Christian) and salient outgroup members (e.g., Republicans). Together, these findings suggest that perceptions of identity overlap are shaped by social environments and identify perceived social support as one mechanism through which social environments influence these perceptions.

title: The Impact of Religiosity on Suicidality in the Autistic Population: The Mediating Role  of Perceived Stress
description: This study examined the relationship between religiosity and suicidality in autistic adults, with a particular focus on whether perceived stress mediates this relationship. Prior research suggests that autistic individuals are at increased risk of suicidal thoughts and behaviours, yet the mechanisms underlying this vulnerability are not fully understood. While religiosity has been identified as a potential protective factor in the general population, its role within autistic populations has received limited attention. A secondary data analysis was conducted on data from 127 autistic adults aged 19-73 years. Measures included self-reported religiosity, perceived stress, suicidality, and additional psychosocial variables such as loneliness, psychological distress, social anxiety, social support, and contextual stressors. Pearson correlation analyses, mediation analysis, and multiple regression were performed. The findings indicated that perceived stress did not significantly mediate the relationship between religiosity and suicidality. Furthermore, religiosity was not identified as a significant predictor of suicidality within this sample. However, other factors, including loneliness, psychological distress, and social anxiety, showed stronger associations with increased suicidality, while social support appeared to play a protective role. Moreover, psychological distress and treatment/health difficulties were found to be significant predictors of suicidality. These results suggest that, although religiosity may offer benefits for some individuals, it does not seem to play a central role in reducing suicide risk among autistic adults. Instead, interventions targeting emotional distress, social isolation, and stress management may be more effective. This study emphasises the importance of focusing on broader psychosocial factors to better understand and reduce suicidality in the autistic population.
